Abstract
Artificial intelligence has dramatically changed real-time video application use across a variety of fields, from surveillance 
and autonomous systems. However, these AI models have high computational demands, and thus high energy consumption, 
limiting scalability in power-constrained environments. This paper systematically addresses energy optimization in real-time 
video inference by exploring energy-performance trade-offs with sophisticated AI models, i.e., YOLOv8 and MobileNet. 
A variety of techniques, such as model pruning, quantization, and hardware-aware optimizations, were stringently evalu-
ated. Experimental results indicate that model pruning resulted in a reduction in energy expenditure by up to 35% without 
compromising detection accuracy to 92%. Moreover, quantization resulted in a further energy saving by 18% and improved 
inference acceleration by 25% with minimal reduction in accuracy. Moreover, reducing frame rates from 30 frames per second 
(FPS) to 15 FPS resulted in a power reduction by 40% with a mere reduction in detection performance by 3%. Benchmarking 
across different hardware setups showed that power savings by optimized lightweight models running in edge devices were 
by as much as 50% compared to GPUs. These results highlight feasible directions for energy efficient AI system design in 
real-time video applications, which prove to be particularly useful in edge computing and Internet of Things environments.
Keywords  Real-time video processing · Energy optimization · AI models · Edge computing · Quantization

1  Introduction
Real-time video processing is an essential building block in 
modern applications in various domains, including autono-
mous systems, healthcare systems, surveillance systems, and 
agricultural systems [1]. Such systems apply advanced algo-
rithms in computer vision relying on artificial intelligence to 
process video streams, detect patterns, and present action-
able results in real time [2]. However, these systems have 
computationally demanding requirements that often lead to 
increased power consumption in most environments, includ-
ing in constrained environments where systems operate in 
mobile systems, IoT systems, and edge systems [3–5].
Energy efficiency is an essential consideration in design-
ing efficient and scalable systems for processing video with 
artificial intelligence. High energy consumption not only 
raises operation costs but also limits the functionality of 
these systems in power-constrained environments where 
power consumption should be minimized in remote sensing 
or battery-powered systems. Additionally, the environmental 
impacts related to energy consumption, especially increased 
carbon emissions, have increased the importance of energy-
aware systems in the domain of AI [6]. Despite these limi-
tations, most work related to video processing with AI has 
been focusing mostly on speed and accuracy while ignoring 
energy efficiency and leaving an immense gap in related 
work in the literature.
The objective is to solve this shortfall by providing rec-
ommendations to boost energy efficiency in processing 
video in real time while not reducing the standards of peak 
performance in the model [7]. Using advanced methods of 
optimizing by applying model pruning, quantization, and 
hardware-aware setups in this work provides an extensive 
evaluation of the relationship between processing speed, 
energy efficiency, and overall performance [8]. This work

2  Related work
2.1  Pruning and quantization techniques
The field of artificial intelligence-related energy efficiency 
has been extensively studied employing different optimiza-
tion approaches at the model level. In particular, pruning 
[9] and quantization [10, 11] were recognized as two impor-
tant approaches. Pruning is the removal of unnecessary or 
redundant parameters from a neural network, which results 
in decreased model size and computational requirements 
with preserved accuracy. On the other hand, quantization 
is the reduction of numerical precision of the weights of 
a model, which accordingly decreases memory need and 
power consumption, particularly during inference [12, 13].
A major breakthrough here is the work of Han et al. 
[14], who introduced the idea of Deep Compression, which 
integrates both pruning and quantization under a single 
paradigm. The approach they described showed that signifi-
cant amounts of energy can be saved without losses to the 
accuracy of the model. These approaches were especially 
beneficial for the deployment of deep learning models on 
embedded and mobile systems that are running under power-
constricted environments.
2.2  Hardware‑aware optimization
Along with model-optimized approaches, there is increas-
ing interest in ones that consider hardware as well. The 
TVM [15] and TensorRT [16] frameworks enable artificial 
intelligence models to adapt to specific hardware configura-
tions through utilization of device-specific features, e.g., the 
number of GPU core units and tensor accelerators. These 
tools improve inference efficiency by minimizing latency 
and power consumption.
However, these approaches tend to require significant 
modification and tuning to perform best, and they might 
show limited generalizability across different hardware sys-
tems. Despite these weaknesses, hardware-aware optimi-
zation remains a key strategy for deploying deep learning 
systems in many resource-limited environments at the edge.
2.3  Lightweight models and video‑specific 
adaptation
Despite the remarkable accuracy achieved by state-of-the-art 
architectures like YOLOv8 [17, 18] and EfficientNet [19], 
these models tend to carry significant power consumption, 
which makes them less desirable for power-constrained sys-
tems. Alternatively, light models like MobileNet [20] and 
ShuffleNet [21] remain widely used for edge AI because of 
their low parameter numbers, combined with efficient use of 
depthwise separable convolutions. Even if these models are 
not necessarily representative of the best accuracy perfor-
mance, they set a solid baseline against which to compare 
energy-efficient optimizations, particularly where hardware 
restrictions are relevant.
Additional challenges facing these applications are 
caused by the spatiotemporal characteristics inherent within 
the video data. The use of adaptive approaches, such as reso-
lution reduction and frame dropping, has been studied for 
reducing computational load during times of sparse data [22, 
23]. These methods successfully reduce power use, but they 
can compromise detection accuracy if high space or time 
fidelity is required.
In addressing these challenges, recent advancements 
within the fields of object detection and tracking placed a 
significant emphasis on robustness against suboptimal video 
settings. This is especially relevant for aerial datasets and 
small object scenarios, as illustrated by datasets within Vis-
Drone and Stanford Drone challenges. For instance, AVL-
Track [24] proposes a dynamic sparse learning approach for 
the purpose of vision-language tracking, whereas research 
within [25] has investigated coordination within multidrone 
systems toward enhancing viewpoint consistency. The track-
ing of small objects has benefited by a significant improve-
ment through the use of wavelet- and graph-based classifica-
tion approaches, as illustrated by SmallTrack [26]. Finally, 
capsule attention mechanisms have shown potential for the 
modeling of spatial as well as spectral features, especially 
under low-resolution environments [27].
Along with these efforts, input-aware inference 
approaches—defined by how a model’s complexity varies

2.4  Research gaps
In light of remarkable progress achieved through discrete 
methodologies for increasing the efficiency of artificial 
intelligence models, a significant gap exists for comprehen-
sive research analyzing the overall impact and interactions 
among the different approaches particularly for real-time 
video processing. Most research usually conducts isolated 
analysis of techniques, thus making it difficult to determine 
overall trade-offs between energy efficiency, accuracy, and 
latency. This research aims at filling this gap by presenting 
an extensive analysis of energy-performance trade-offs for 
different optimization approaches, together with produc-
ing practical knowledge for applying AI models on limited 
resources environments, with a special reference to real-time 
video applications.
3  Materials and methods
3.1  Dataset description
The dataset used within this research was carefully sourced 
from a wide variety of publicly available sources to ensure an 
extensive and diversified collection of real-world examples 
within the video processing domain. The primary sources 
included large sets of videos used within benchmarks for 
object tracking and object detection to ensure compatibility 
with the standard criteria used within the evaluation process. 
The sources used were based on their compatibility to the 
aforementioned criteria, along with other practical issues 
within artificial intelligence, such as object densities, move-
ment complexities, and interference.
The dataset included video sequences from the AI City 
Challenge dataset [29] consisting of high-definition record-
ings made to observe traffic behavior along with carefully 
hand-labeled annotations to enable vehicle tracking and 
detection. The dataset was especially helpful to test the 
method of optimality within the framework of real-world 
urban traffic dynamics that are plagued by varying object 
densities. The VisDrone dataset [30] was also used to test 
the efficacy of monitoring via aerial means under various 
scenarios, because the dataset included a wide variety of 
urban- and rural-related annotations. The Stanford Drone 
Dataset [31] was used to test under independent conditions 
to ensure the generalizability of the measures. The video 
sequences from the Open Images Dataset [32] were also 
used to enable the measurement of classes other than the 
vehicle class and pedestrian class to ensure the collection of 
supplementary evidence to test under generalized contexts. 
A thorough classification of the datasets under various con-
texts is presented in greater detail within Table  1.
Each series of frames was labeled with bounding boxes 
representing object context, with corresponding class labels 
in the same object context, and added temporal frame-level 
context to support an overall evaluation of tracking and 
object detection effectiveness. All these annotations con-
formed to PASCAL VOC standards by adopting an Intersec-
tion over Union value of 0.5 in determining mean average 
precision [33]. This is to support valid comparison with the 
previous work. Figures (see Figs.  1, 2, 3 and 4) provide 
sample frames in the dataset to reflect variation in scene 
difficulty, object number, and atmospheric factors.
To guarantee diversity in the dataset, it was segmented 
systemically into various categories, including static views, 
motion-intensive activities, and complicated scenery 
with overlapping items. Traffic monitoring sequences, for 
instance, featured cars driving in various velocities while 
indoor and outdoor surveillance captured various lighting 
conditions. Videos in agricultural environments captured 
moving animals in addition to dynamic changes in the 
background generated by vehicles and equipment. Table  2 
illustrates an extensive breakdown of categories in the data-
set including an average number of items in each frame in 
addition to motion complexity.
While the overall goal in working with this dataset was to 
analyze methods to improve energy efficiency, this was also 
used to test speed and accuracy of inference in diverse condi-
tions. Low-density vs. high-density environments in terms 
of energy consumption was compared to determine compu-
tational requirements in response to object density. Videos 
with intense motion complexity, frequent scene changes, 
or rapid movements have been used to seriously challenge 
the performance of these models in dynamic conditions. A

3.2  Models description
The advanced algorithms used in this research were 
selected based on their proven efficiency in real-time 
object detection and classification in the context of video 
processing methods. This research used two popular 
architectures, MobileNet [20] and YOLOv8 [17, 18], to 
investigate different optimizations in different topologi-
cal setups characteristic of the architecture. YOLOv8 is 
a high-throughput convolution neural network (CNN) 
specially optimized for real-time object detection, while 
MobileNet is an efficiency-driven framework widely used 
in mobile and edge AI applications due to its lightweight 
nature, low parameter footprint, and support for depthwise 
separable convolutions, which provide a dramatic reduc-
tion in the amount of multiply accumulate operations. The 
use of linear bottleneck features and width multipliers ena-
bles implementation on hardware with limited resources,

YOLOv8 operates in the context of single-shot detection 
to avoid the use of region proposal networks by predicting 
bounding boxes and classes in a single forward pass. This 
model has an attribute backbone to achieve efficient flow 
of gradients while reducing computational redundancy. 
Additionally, an upsampling module is used to support 
multi-scale feature fusion, while an object head is used to 
approximate object locations with corresponding confidence 
scores. CSPDarkNet [34] is used in the backbone to main-
tain efficient flow while reducing computational redundancy. 
Additionally, an upsampling module uses PAN layers to sup-
port efficient transfer between scales. Owing to its complex 
design, YOLOv8 requires extensive computational resources 
to support in systems where power consumption is an issue 
to avoid power consumption.
In contrast, MobileNet has been specially developed to be 
efficient by reducing both the number of parameters required 
by the model as well as during inference floating-point oper-
ations [20]. This model is developed through an inverted 
residual design that uses linear bottlenecks to maintain com-
putational efficiency while ensuring stable feature represen-
tation in tandem. One key design element in MobileNet is 
the width multiplier that allows dynamic changes in every 
convolution layer to change channels to achieve an efficient 
balance between effectiveness and efficiency in proportion 
to the resources in the hardware.

3.3.1  Model pruning
Model pruning has been established to be an efficient tech-
nique to reduce the number of parameters in deep neural 
networks by getting rid of redundant or secondary weights 
[35]. This not only results in computational cost savings 
but reduces memory requirements as well, thus improving 
power efficiency.

To analyze in an organized manner the efficacy of trim-

restore performance compromised by the trimming of these 
weights. This process was implemented to maintain stabil-
ity in the capacity of the neural network to perform feature

3.3.3  Hardware‑aware configurations
To further enhance energy efficiency, we optimized model 
execution based on hardware-specific features. Techniques, 
such as TensorRT optimization, CUDA graph execution, and 
mixed-precision training, were employed.
The speedup factor S of hardware-aware optimization can 
be estimated using the following equation:
where Tbaseline and Toptimized represent the inference times 
before and after optimization, respectively. A higher S value 
indicates a greater improvement in inference speed, directly 
correlating with reduced execution latency and enhanced 
real-time processing capabilities [38].
TensorRT optimization is a key technique utilized to 
accelerate deep learning inference by transforming high-
level model representations into an optimized execution 
graph tailored for NVIDIA hardware [39]. This process 
involves multiple optimization steps, including layer fusion, 
precision calibration, kernel auto-tuning, and memory layout 
transformations, all aimed at maximizing utilization of the 
GPU architecture.
CUDA graph execution was also employed to minimize 
the overhead associated with kernel launches and memory 
transfers. Instead of invoking computational kernels indi-
vidually for each inference pass, CUDA graph execution 
enables the recording and execution of a predefined compu-
tation graph, eliminating redundant memory allocations and 
reducing execution overhead. This technique is particularly 
effective in batch processing scenarios where repeated oper-
ations can be pre-scheduled for execution, ensuring optimal 
use of compute resources.
Mixed precision inference leverages the ability of mod-
ern GPUs to efficiently process lower-precision computa-
tions using dedicated Tensor Cores. In this study, automatic 
mixed precision (AMP) was integrated into the inference 
pipeline, enabling the selective use of FP16 arithmetic

The integration of hardware-aware optimizations requires 
a structured deployment pipeline, including model conver-

trained in high-level frameworks such as PyTorch and Ten-

Finally, execution traces were analyzed using profiling tools, 
such as NVIDIA Nsight Systems and nvprof, allowing for 
detailed evaluation of kernel performance, memory access 
patterns, and floating-point operation efficiency.
3.3.4  Combined optimization effect
The integrated optimality technique blends model prun-
ing, quantization, and hardware-aware setups to realize an 
optimum balance between computational efficiency and 
performance in the models. Though each methodology is 
efficient in reducing energy consumption, inference delay, 
and computational complexity in an isolated manner, collec-
tive effectiveness provides an integrated system efficient in 
various forms of hardware deployments. When these meth-
ods are used in an organized sequence in systematic order, 
improving energy efficiency is achieved while not affecting 
deployed-model performance.
3.4  Implementation details
All experiments were run on two different hardware plat-
forms to accurately replicate both high-performance com-
puting and edge computing environments. The first platform 
used was an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80 GB of RAM and 
CUDA support version 12.1, while the second platform used 
was an NVIDIA Jetson Nano with 4 GB of RAM running 
JetPack version 4.6. All processes related to model devel-
opment and training were conducted using Python version 
3.10 along with PyTorch version 2.1.0. Later, the trained 
models were exported as ONNX and optimized using Ten-
sorRT version 8.6 to enable hardware-aware inference on 
both platforms. Before exporting the model, structured prun-
ing and quantization methods—namely INT8 and FP16—
were applied, and the model execution was profiled using 
NVIDIA Nsight Systems and nvprof to assess inference 
latency and energy consumption.
The dataset we employed for the present research 
included about 450,000 annotated frames sourced from 
four publicly available data sets: AI City Challenge, Vis-
Drone, Stanford Drone Dataset, and Open Images V6. The 
frames were distributed among three different subsets: train-
ing frames (70%) with a total of 315,000, validation frames 
(15%) with a total of 67,500, and test frames (15%) with a 
total of 67,500. Efforts were made to keep all subsets uni-
form regarding object class distributions, motions, and scene 
complexities. In addition, certain data augmentation opera-
tions were applied for training robustness enhancement, 
including random cropping with bounding box dimension 
ranges of up to 10%, horizontal flipping with a probability of 
50%, color jittering with ±20% variation ranges for bright-
ness and contrast, and the addition of Gaussian noise with a 
standard deviation of 0.01, among other operations.
Both the YOLOv8 and MobileNet architectures were fine-
tuned using the Adam optimization algorithm with a learn-
ing rate starting at 0.001, then adjusted following a cosine 
decay schedule later on. Batch size was set to 32 on the 
A100 GPU and 8 on the Jetson Nano, respecting memory 
capacity restrictions. The training was maintained for up 
to 100 epochs, with early stopping mechanisms enabled 
after 10 consecutive epochs showed no reductions in vali-
dation loss. The training procedure was applied to a set of 
500 representative frames from the training set to achieve 
uniform scaling across varying input scenarios. The evalua-
tion metrics included detection accuracy (mAP@0.5), infer-
ence latency (in milliseconds per frame), power utilization 
(in millijoules per frame), and processing throughputs (in 
frames per second). While the source video streams ranged 
between a rate of 15 to 60 frames per second, all experiments 
were strictly normalized and averaged at a fixed rate of 30 
frames per second over the course of 500 frames.
4  Experimental results
The study was done by analyzing an assortment of diverse 
datasets to analyze their impacts in respect to energy effi-
ciency, speed in making inferences, and modeling perfor-
mance in live video processing. The dataset included high-
definition video sequences between frame rates of 15 to 60 
frames per second used in diverse purposes including obser-
vation in traffic flow and agricultural work. The datasets 
included diverse extents of concentration in objects, motion 
complexities, and climatic factors, thus providing an ideal 
benchmark dataset to various methods of optimality.
The impact of pruning on retained energy consumption 
and accuracy was compared over various dataset classes. As 
can be seen in Figs. 7 and 8, sparsifying to a sparsity value 
of 30% by means of pruning decreased energy consumption 
by 35% while retaining an accuracy value of 92%. However, 
in crowded environments where multiple objects overlap in 
each frame, over-pruning over 50% led to an abrupt fall in 
accuracy. This was especially true in traffic dataset classes 
where overlapping among crowded objects required an

5  Discussion
The present research emphasizes the importance of an opti-
mality pipeline to enhance computational efficiency and 
save energy during real-time video processing using the 
techniques of deep learning. With the use of systematic 
techniques like pruning, quantization, and hardware opti-
mizations, there are large savings possible in computational 
complexity along with energy consumption, keeping the 
object recognition performance within an acceptable range.
The process of thinning the model, done through prun-
ing, dramatically reduces unnecessary computational loads; 
the efficacy of the process varies based on the complexity 
of the information and the organization of the components 
within the information. In sparse scenes that include static 
backdrops, extensive pruning can be done with little loss of 
accuracy. However, where the scenes are dense and dynamic, 
the need arises to be more careful with strategies. The quan-
tization method also improves efficiency, INT8 being the 
best trade-off between energy savings and precision. Even 
though INT4 offers higher energy savings, the use of INT4 
for video-related applications causes a sharp drop in preci-
sion, thus limiting the use to real-world applications.
Optimizations grounded in hardware characteristics are 
crucial to the improvements seen in performance, the ben-
efits being highly reliant upon the specific nature of the spe-
cialized hardware components like the Tensor Cores and 
the bandwidth of the memory. While GPUs allow for per-
formance improvements, energy-efficient options like the 
Jetson Nano place restrictions that mean the careful use of 
optimization techniques specific to the specific system under 
test are required.
A central problem in current research is the balance 
between model performance and the ability to detect. 
Over-compression will impede the identification of small 
or occluded objects within complex scenes, highlight-
ing the need for adaptive techniques that adapt model 
complexity based on the nature of the input data and the 
computational resources available. Future research will be 
required to address the use of adaptive pruning, scalable 
quantization, and graph dynamics reorganization as means 
to adapt artificial intelligence models to various deployment 
environments.
The current research supports earlier findings regarding the 
efficiency of deep learning inference and underscores the need 
for adaptive optimization techniques that balance performance 
measures with power usage. Future innovation is envisioned to 
depend on scalable precision methods and hardware-focused 
artificial intelligence pipelines. A consequent next step, based 
on the insights laid out here, is to apply the optimization pro-
cess elaborated on here-pruning, quantization, and hardware-
aware inference-to state-of-the-art lightweight architectures 
like EfficientNet-lite and MobileViT. These models introduce

synergies relevant to the optimization of power consumption. 
Such benchmarking activities will also allow architecture level 
Pareto frontiers to be created that compare power efficiency 
with accuracy on different hardware platforms and deployment 
scenarios.
Simultaneous with architectural design and configuration 
strategy development, future research efforts should address 
low-level hardware controls for edge computing platforms, 
represented by the NVIDIA Jetson line of products. These 
platforms allow for a granular degree of system operation by 
supporting CPU core number adjustments and CPU, GPU, 
and Embedded Memory Controller (EMC) frequency scal-
ing. Changes to these settings can greatly impact processing 
latency and power consumption efficiency, especially under 
adaptive or context-aware processing scenarios. Inclusion of 
these hardware dynamic adjustments within the optimization 
framework described within this work would lead to mini-
mized response times for changing computational workloads 
and enhanced deployment effectiveness. Understanding the 
interactions between software compression approaches and 
hardware runtime settings is a key next step toward develop-
ing viable, power-efficient cognitive systems.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence has dramatically changed real-time video application use across a variety of fields, from surveillance and autonomous systems. However, these AI models have high computational demands, and thus high energy consumption, limiting scalability in power-constrained environments. This paper systematically addresses energy optimization in real-time video inference by exploring energy-performance trade-offs with sophisticated AI models, i.e., YOLOv8 and MobileNet. A variety of techniques, such as model pruning, quantization, and hardware-aware optimizations, were stringently evalu- ated. Experimental results indicate that model pruning resulted in a reduction in energy expenditure by up to 35% without compromising detection accuracy to 92%. Moreover, quantization resulted in a further energy saving by 18% and improved inference acceleration by 25% with minimal reduction in accuracy. Moreover, reducing frame rates from 30 frames per second (FPS) to 15 FPS resulted in a power reduction by 40% with a mere reduction in detection performance by 3%. Benchmarking across different hardware setups showed that power savings by optimized lightweight models running in edge devices were by as much as 50% compared to GPUs. These results highlight feasible directions for energy efficient AI system design in real-time video applications, which prove to be particularly useful in edge computing and Internet of Things environments.
